slots.practicalActivity: Write three architecture principles your own organization's (or a realistic hypothetical one's) governance program should follow, each as a one-sentence rule with a one-sentence rationale (for example, 'classification tags travel with the data, not with a separate wiki page -- because disconnected documentation drifts out of date'). Then sketch a simple reference architecture diagram showing source systems, a governed layer, and consumption, labeling where each principle would actually apply.
slots.deliverable: Three written architecture principles with rationale, plus a sketched reference architecture diagram labeling where each principle applies.

slots.practicalActivity: Fill out a governance capabilities map for a real or hypothetical organization: list the eight to ten capabilities the lesson names (cataloging, classification, lineage, access control, quality, and so on) and mark each as Present, Partial, or Missing today. Then write one paragraph on how your organization's operating model -- centralized, federated, or decentralized -- would change who is responsible for closing each 'Missing' gap.
slots.deliverable: A completed governance capabilities map with present/partial/missing status, plus a written note on operating-model fit for closing gaps.

slots.practicalActivity: For your own organization, write one paragraph arguing for a centralized governance model and a second paragraph arguing for a federated model, each naming a real structural fact about the organization (number of business units, how distributed the data ownership already is) that supports that choice -- then state which one you'd actually recommend and why.
slots.deliverable: Two written one-paragraph arguments (centralized and federated) plus a final recommendation with its deciding factor named.

slots.practicalActivity: Write one paragraph explaining the real difference between decentralized governance and data mesh governance (decentralization alone has no shared standards; data mesh adds federated computational governance and treats each domain's output as a data product with an SLA). Then name one domain from your own organization that could realistically own its data as a product under a mesh model, and one it couldn't yet, and why.
slots.deliverable: A written comparison of decentralized versus data-mesh governance, plus one domain that could and one that couldn't adopt data-product ownership yet.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-page data product specification for the domain you named last hour as mesh-ready: its name, its owner, its documented interface (schema, update frequency, quality SLA), and who consumes it. Then run your organization through the lesson's model-selection criteria (number of domains, maturity, regulatory pressure) and state, in writing, which single operating model you'd actually recommend today.
slots.deliverable: A one-page data product specification plus a final governance-model recommendation with its selection criteria stated.

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch an enterprise metadata architecture diagram showing at least three real source systems feeding one catalog layer, then write one paragraph deciding between a single enterprise catalog versus a catalog-of-catalogs federation pattern for your organization, naming how many distinct platforms (SQL Server, Snowflake, Databricks, Fabric) it would actually need to span.
slots.deliverable: A sketched enterprise metadata architecture diagram plus a written single-catalog-versus-federation decision with its reasoning.

slots.practicalActivity: Diagram a lineage path for one real report or dashboard you know, from its source table through every transformation hop to the final visual, then write how you'd integrate that lineage across two different platforms if the source and the report lived in different tools. Finally, write one active-metadata trigger you'd want configured (for example, automatically flagging a table for re-review when its upstream schema changes) and what action it should fire.
slots.deliverable: A diagrammed lineage path across at least one platform boundary, plus one written active-metadata trigger-and-action rule.

slots.practicalActivity: Metadata architecture lab: combine the enterprise metadata diagram, the catalog-integration decision, the lineage path, and the active-metadata trigger from the last two slots into one metadata architecture proposal for your organization, then write a one-paragraph case for why this architecture would have caught or shortened a real data-trust incident (made up or real) faster than a disconnected wiki-style catalog would have.
slots.deliverable: One consolidated metadata architecture proposal plus a written case for its real-world value against a disconnected-documentation baseline.

slots.practicalActivity: Design an access control architecture diagram for one sensitive data domain: the classification tiers it uses, where role-based access is enforced (at the warehouse layer, the catalog layer, or both), and how a least-privilege exception request would actually flow through it. Name the real platform (Snowflake, Databricks Unity Catalog, Fabric, Purview) that would own enforcement at each layer.
slots.deliverable: An access control architecture diagram naming the enforcement layer and platform for one sensitive data domain, plus its exception-request path.

lessons.title: Platform Architecture: Purview, Fabric, Databricks and Snowflake

slots.practicalActivity: Write one governance rule from this course as policy-as-code pseudocode (a tagging or access rule expressed as an if/then statement rather than a prose policy document). Then, for your own organization's actual platform mix, write one sentence per platform it runs (Purview, Fabric, Databricks, Snowflake, or none) naming each one's governance reach from narrowest to widest, and which one -- if any -- you'd need as the cross-platform layer.
slots.deliverable: One policy-as-code rule expressed as pseudocode, plus a written platform-reach assessment for your own organization's real platform mix.

slots.practicalActivity: Governance automation lab: take the policy-as-code rule you wrote last hour and design the automated enforcement around it -- what triggers the check (a scheduled job, a new-table event), what happens on a violation (an alert, a blocked access grant, a flagged catalog entry), and who gets notified. Write it as a short automation runbook, not just a policy statement.
slots.deliverable: A written governance automation runbook naming the trigger, the enforcement action on violation, and the notified owner.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-page governance architecture strategy for your organization covering current state (today's real platform mix and gaps), target state (the architecture you've been designing across this course), and a phased roadmap of at least three stages to get from one to the other, each stage naming what becomes possible that wasn't before.
slots.deliverable: A one-page written governance architecture strategy with current state, target state, and a three-stage roadmap.

slots.practicalActivity: Write one architecture decision record (ADR) for the single biggest architectural choice you made in this course (your operating model choice, your catalog-integration pattern, or your platform recommendation): the context, the options you considered, the decision, and the consequences -- then note where that ADR would live in your overall governance architecture documentation set.
slots.deliverable: One complete, real architecture decision record (context, options, decision, consequences) for a choice made earlier in this course.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a governance architecture review board charter: who sits on it (naming real roles, not just titles), what triggers a mandatory review (a new platform adoption, a cross-domain data product, a major access-model change), and what a review actually checks for using your own ADR template as the submission format.
slots.deliverable: A written review board charter naming its members, its review triggers, and the ADR-based submission format it requires.

lessons.title: Governance Architecture Case Study: Global Manufacturer
Governance Architecture Case Study: Financial Services

slots.practicalActivity: Compare the two case studies in writing: what operating model and platform choice each organization made and why their industry (manufacturing versus financial services) drove a different answer. Then write one paragraph on which case study's architecture is closer to your own organization's real constraints, and what you'd borrow directly from it.
slots.deliverable: A written comparison of both case studies' architecture choices, plus a paragraph naming which one fits your own organization best.

slots.practicalActivity: Full architecture lab: assemble everything from this course into one architecture package for your organization -- the reference architecture diagram, the operating model recommendation, the metadata/catalog architecture, the access control design, one ADR, and the phased roadmap -- as a single package a new governance architect could pick up and extend.
slots.deliverable: One consolidated governance architecture package covering diagram, operating model, metadata/catalog design, access control, an ADR, and a roadmap.

slots.practicalActivity: Deliver (recorded, or live to a colleague/mentor) a 10-minute presentation of your full governance architecture package: the current-state problem, the target architecture diagram, the operating model decision, and the phased roadmap, ending with one specific ask for what would need approval to move to stage one.
slots.deliverable: A recorded or witnessed 10-minute architecture presentation ending in one specific, decidable ask.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can design a complete enterprise governance architecture for a real organization -- choosing and justifying an operating model, designing the metadata/catalog and lineage layer, architecting access control and policy-as-code enforcement, mapping real platforms like Purview, Fabric, Databricks and Snowflake to the right governance reach, and presenting the whole target-state architecture and roadmap to a review board -- the most senior, architecture-level skill in this career path.
